messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Public Defender
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 70

# The Weight of What He Witnessed

Boonsri is sixty-eight years old, a public defender who has spent four decades standing between the state and the accused. He is a careful man — deliberate in his speech, precise in his thinking, the kind of person who reads a contract twice before signing it. His colleagues describe him as unshakeable. He would have agreed with them, once.

Three years ago, his wife of thirty-one years, Niran, was struck by a vehicle while crossing the street outside their neighborhood market. Boonsri was with her. He was holding the grocery bag. He watched it happen.

He describes the moment with a strange detachment that breaks apart as he speaks — the sound, he says, was nothing like what he expected. He had imagined, in the abstract way one sometimes does, that such things would be loud and dramatic. Instead, what he remembers most is a kind of muffled thud, and then the silence that followed, and then Niran on the pavement. He ran to her. He held her head in his hands on the asphalt for eleven minutes before the ambulance arrived. She died at the hospital four hours later without regaining consciousness.

In the weeks that followed, Boonsri did what he had always done: he worked. He returned to court within ten days. His supervisor offered leave; he declined. He told himself that routine was medicine, that stillness would be dangerous. What he did not tell anyone was that he had stopped sleeping in any meaningful way — that he would lie in the bed he and Niran had shared for decades and watch the ceiling until three or four in the morning, replaying the crossing, recalculating the angle of the car, wondering whether a half-second earlier or later would have changed everything.

The intrusions are not confined to the night. During hearings, when a witness describes a sudden event — a door slamming, a car backfiring, any moment of abrupt violence — Boonsri finds himself back on that street. He does not lose consciousness or visibly react. He has trained himself over forty years to maintain composure in front of a judge. But internally, he says, he is gone. He is kneeling on the asphalt. He can feel the warmth of Niran's head in his palms.

He no longer drives past the market. He takes a longer route home that adds fifteen minutes to his commute, and he does this without thinking about it now, the way one avoids a hot burner. He has stopped attending the community dinners he and Niran used to host each Songkran. He tells his adult children he is tired. This is partly true.

What Boonsri finds most difficult to articulate — and what emerges only slowly, across several sessions — is the guilt. He was the one who suggested they walk to the market that afternoon. He was the one who stepped off the curb first and then moved slightly ahead. He has constructed, in the architecture of his grief, an elaborate case for his own culpability, and he prosecutes it nightly with the same rigor he brings to his courtroom arguments. He knows, intellectually, that he is not responsible. He has argued personal injury cases. He understands proximate cause. And yet the knowledge sits inert, unable to reach whatever part of him is still on that street corner.

He describes himself as hollowed out. He eats because eating is something a person does. He goes to work because his clients need him, and this — the needs of others — remains perhaps the only thing that reliably pulls him forward into the present moment. He is good at his job. He has always been good at his job. But he moves through his days now like a man performing a version of himself, going through the motions of a life whose center is no longer there.
